content: 1. Pregnant women attending antenatal clinics in high HIV prevalence settings should be routinely offered HIV testing. This includes offering testing to all couples, male partners, and infants exposed to HIV. In other settings with high antenatal care (ANC) coverage, countries should also consider routine HIV testing for pregnant women, with a focus on testing male partners of women with HIV and HIV-exposed infants. In low-prevalence settings with limited resources and low ANC and HIV testing coverage, geographic prioritization based on HIV prevalence may be considered. Repeat testing for HIV-negative pregnant women is recommended during the third trimester or early in the postnatal and breastfeeding period, but only in high-prevalence settings. In low-prevalence settings, one HIV test per pregnancy may suffice, while in high-prevalence settings, additional testing during the postpartum or breastfeeding period may be necessary. Dual testing for HIV and syphilis should be prioritized to eliminate both infections. 2. HIV testing is critical for key populations and their partners, as these groups often have significantly higher HIV prevalence compared to the general population. Focused HIV testing services (HTS) may also be considered for other priority populations with high prevalence or incidence, such as adolescent females and young women in hyperendemic settings, military personnel, and migrant workers in sub-Saharan Africa. Special attention should be given to migrant populations originating from high-prevalence countries, ensuring testing is offered in line with WHO's 5 Cs (consent, confidentiality, counseling, correct results, and connection to care). HIV testing should be offered at least annually to key populations and other vulnerable groups with ongoing HIV risk, depending on local prevalence and incidence. HTS should be tailored to meet the needs and preferences of key populations, such as offering flexible hours or combining HIV testing with testing for hepatitis B and C, sexually transmitted infections (STIs), and tuberculosis (TB), as co-infections are common. 3. Testing the partners and family members of individuals with HIV (index case-based testing) is highly effective, as approximately half of the primary sexual partners of people with HIV are also likely to be infected. Similarly, children of HIV-positive adults have higher rates of HIV infection compared to the general population. This approach is cost-effective and identifies a high proportion of HIV-positive cases, but implementation gaps remain widespread. In some settings, with the consent of the individual, contact tracing, partner notification services, or voluntary partner testing facilitation may be considered. 4. In high HIV prevalence settings, HIV testing should be prioritized for TB patients, with a focus on identifying co-infected individuals and ensuring immediate referral for TB treatment followed by antiretroviral therapy (ART) within two weeks. This approach significantly reduces mortality. WHO also recommends HIV testing for the partners of TB patients and index case-based testing for other family members, as this is likely to yield high results for its cost. In low HIV prevalence settings with high TB and HIV co-infection rates, integrated TB/HIV services are essential to reduce loss to follow-up and improve care. Offering HIV testing to all TB patients can enhance HIV surveillance among this population. 5. Countries should prioritize HIV testing within STI services, as these clinics provide an effective entry point for reaching men and key populations at high risk of HIV infection. Integrating HIV testing into STI services can increase coverage among these groups. 6. HIV testing should be routinely offered in harm reduction services, including drug treatment programs, needle and syringe programs, and opioid substitution therapy programs. 7. HIV testing should be guided by indicator conditions, such as malnutrition in children, as these conditions are often associated with higher HIV prevalence. Recent European guidelines recommend routine HIV testing for individuals presenting with specific indicator conditions where HIV prevalence is significantly higher than in the general population. 8. HIV self-testing (HIVST) is an emerging approach that can be targeted to specific populations or made widely accessible to reach individuals who are reluctant or unable to access traditional HIV testing services. HIVST is particularly beneficial for key populations, individuals at high risk of HIV acquisition, and those requiring frequent retesting, such as serodiscordant couples. All reactive HIV self-test results must be confirmed at a healthcare facility. 9. In countries with regions of varying HIV prevalence and incidence, focusing HIV testing services in areas with the highest HIV burden, such as transport hubs, mining, and fishing communities, can be efficient. Geographic prioritization has been used in some countries with low overall HIV burden but highly concentrated epidemics to introduce phased scale-up of HIV testing services. 10. In high-prevalence settings, routine provider-initiated testing and counseling (PITC) should be offered to all adults, adolescents, and children in primary care settings. This approach has increased the proportion of people who know their HIV status but is limited to those who seek care at health facilities. 11. Facility prioritization during the scale-up of HIV testing services should be considered, as evidence shows that the proportion of HIV-positive cases identified varies significantly among facilities. Facilities in low-prevalence areas often have low identification rates due to barriers such as inappropriate hours, long wait times, stigma, and discrimination. 12. Multi-disease campaigns that integrate HIV testing with other health services can reduce stigma and discrimination while reaching populations that may not otherwise test for HIV. However, the proportion of HIV-positive cases identified in such campaigns varies and should be assessed for efficiency. 13. Non-coercive, on-site workplace testing in areas of high HIV prevalence and low testing coverage can reach men and women who may not utilize health services. However, potential risks such as stigma, discrimination, and breaches of confidentiality must be considered, along with ensuring post-test access to care and treatment. 14. HIV testing in educational institutions may be considered in hyperendemic settings, but experience with school-based approaches is limited. Issues of consent, confidentiality, stigma, and linkage to prevention and care services acceptable to adolescents and young people must be addressed before implementation. 15. Standalone voluntary counseling and testing (VCT) facilities, whether fixed or mobile, can be effective in reaching undiagnosed individuals, particularly in underserved areas or populations. These facilities should focus on areas with low access to health services, such as rural populations and men. 16. Door-to-door HIV testing in high-prevalence settings with low testing coverage can help identify undiagnosed individuals. This approach should consider cost, accessibility, and linkage to care, treatment, and prevention, especially in rural or hard-to-reach areas. Delivery tactics, such as weekend and evening visits, can help reach men with limited time for facility-based testing. 17. Mobile testing services should be implemented in communities and populations that are hard to reach, such as key populations, adolescents, and those underserved by the formal health system. These services should focus on specific population groups and areas based on HIV prevalence and ensure linkage to care, treatment, and prevention. 18. Routine HIV testing should be offered to individuals seeking family planning services, as this can reach sexually active populations. 19. In 14 priority countries, HIV testing should be offered to all clients presenting for voluntary medical male circumcision.
